hook.text: Every business decision depends on what competitors, customers, and regulators will do. That's a game.

buildup.text: Game theory gives firms tools to anticipate rivals' moves and choose the best response.

discovery.text: The key insight: your optimal strategy depends on others' strategies, not just your own preferences.

twist.text: But firms don't play once. They interact repeatedly, creating patterns of trust, rivalry, and signaling.

climax.text: From pricing to patents, mergers to marketing, game theory explains why firms behave as they do.

punchline.text: Business is strategy against living opponents.

quiz.question: What makes business a 'game' in game-theoretic terms?

hook.text: Amazon, Uber, and Google all moved first in their markets. Is being first always an advantage?

buildup.text: First movers capture customers, build brand loyalty, and set industry standards before rivals arrive.

discovery.text: In game theory, the first mover 'commits'—forcing competitors to react to a fait accompli.

twist.text: But first movers also bear all the risk and cost. Facebook beat earlier social networks by learning from them.

climax.text: The advantage depends on switching costs. High switching costs reward first movers. Low costs reward fast followers.

punchline.text: First isn't always best. Fastest is.

quiz.question: When is first-mover advantage strongest?

hook.text: Cortés burned his ships after landing in Mexico. His soldiers had no retreat option. They fought harder.

buildup.text: In business, a credible commitment is an irreversible action that changes the game for everyone.

discovery.text: Building a factory commits a firm to a market. Competitors know it won't easily leave, so they adjust.

twist.text: Empty threats are ignored. Only commitments that are costly to reverse change rivals' behavior.

climax.text: Intel's massive chip fab investments commit it to Moore's Law. Competitors assume Intel will keep pushing.

punchline.text: Burning ships is a strategic choice.

quiz.question: What makes a commitment credible?
options: Writing it in a press release

hook.text: Chess masters think from the endgame backward. The best business strategists do the same.

buildup.text: Backward induction starts at the final decision and works backward: 'If they do X last, I should do Y now.'

discovery.text: This technique solves sequential games—any situation where players take turns making decisions.

twist.text: In practice, backward induction assumes perfect rationality. Real players make mistakes, changing the calculus.

climax.text: Firms use it in negotiations: 'If we walk away, they'll accept our offer to avoid losing the deal.'

punchline.text: Think from the end to find the start.

quiz.question: Where does backward induction start?

hook.text: If your rival cuts prices, should you follow or hold? The answer depends on compliance and substitution.

buildup.text: Strategic complements: when your rival does more, your best response is to do more too. Arms races.

discovery.text: Strategic substitutes: when your rival does more, your best response is to do less. Quantity competition.

twist.text: Price competition tends to be complementary (everyone matches cuts). Quantity competition is substitutive.

climax.text: Knowing which type of game you're in determines whether to match, undercut, or hold your ground.

punchline.text: Match or diverge? Know your game type.

quiz.question: What are strategic complements?
options: When doing more prompts rivals to also do more

hook.text: Two gas stations across the street. Whoever is cheaper gets all the customers. Welcome to Bertrand.

buildup.text: In Bertrand competition, firms compete on price. Each one undercuts the other by a penny.

discovery.text: The equilibrium: both firms price at cost, earning zero profit—even with only two competitors.

twist.text: This 'Bertrand paradox' seems extreme, but gas stations, airlines, and telecoms often slash margins this way.

climax.text: Firms escape Bertrand by differentiating: brand, quality, location, or service justify premium pricing.

punchline.text: Price wars end at zero profit.

quiz.question: What is the Bertrand paradox?
options: Two competitors can drive profits to zero

hook.text: What if firms compete on quantity instead of price? Each decides how much to produce, and the market sets the price.

buildup.text: In Cournot competition, producing more lowers the price for everyone. Your gain is partly your rival's loss.

discovery.text: The Nash equilibrium: each firm produces less than the monopoly amount but more than the competitive level.

twist.text: More firms in the market push the outcome closer to perfect competition. Fewer firms mean higher prices.

climax.text: OPEC members play Cournot: each decides oil output, and the global price adjusts accordingly.

punchline.text: How much you make decides what it costs.

quiz.question: What do firms choose in Cournot competition?

hook.text: Airlines charge $200 for a seat one person pays $800 for. Same seat, same flight. Different prices.

buildup.text: Price discrimination means charging different customers different prices based on willingness to pay.

discovery.text: Strategies include: student discounts, early-bird pricing, premium tiers, and geographic pricing.

twist.text: It only works if customers can't resell. You can't buy a cheap student flight and sell it to a business traveler.

climax.text: Perfect price discrimination captures all consumer surplus. In practice, firms approximate it with segmentation.

punchline.text: Same product, different price, more profit.

quiz.question: What prevents price discrimination from working?
options: If customers can resell to each other

hook.text: A large firm drops prices below cost to drive a smaller rival out of business. Then it raises prices.

buildup.text: Predatory pricing is illegal in most countries, but proving intent is notoriously difficult.

discovery.text: The predator loses money short-term but gains monopoly power long-term if the rival exits.

twist.text: Game theory shows predation is often irrational: the losses exceed the gains unless the predator is much larger.

climax.text: Uber lost billions undercutting taxi prices. The strategy assumes competitors eventually give up.

punchline.text: Losing money on purpose is a power play.

quiz.question: Why is predatory pricing risky for the predator?

hook.text: 'We'll match any lower price!' Sounds customer-friendly. It's actually a signal to competitors.

buildup.text: The message to rivals: 'Don't bother cutting prices. We'll match instantly, so you won't steal our customers.'

discovery.text: Price matching softens competition. If everyone matches, nobody gains from cutting. Prices stay high.

twist.text: Economists showed that price matching can function as tacit collusion—without any secret agreement.

climax.text: Regulators struggle: the policy looks pro-consumer, but its strategic effect is anti-competitive.

punchline.text: Matching prices keeps them high.

quiz.question: What is the hidden strategic effect of price matching?
options: It discourages rivals from cutting prices

hook.text: A monopolist sees a new competitor approaching. How can it scare the rival into staying out?

buildup.text: The incumbent can build excess capacity, cut prices, or invest heavily in branding—all costly signals.

discovery.text: The goal: make entry look unprofitable. If the newcomer expects losses, it won't enter.

twist.text: But empty threats don't work. If it's cheaper to accommodate than fight, the new entrant calls the bluff.

climax.text: Only credible commitments deter: investments that lock the incumbent into aggressive post-entry behavior.

punchline.text: Deterrence only works if rivals believe it.

quiz.question: What makes entry deterrence credible?
options: Irreversible investments that commit to fighting

hook.text: An incumbent sets prices low—not to maximize profit, but to make entry look unprofitable to newcomers.

buildup.text: If the market price is low, potential entrants calculate they can't cover their costs and stay out.

discovery.text: Limit pricing sacrifices some current profit to preserve monopoly power and future earnings.

twist.text: It only works if entrants can't tell whether the low price reflects low cost or strategic intent.

climax.text: Walmart's everyday low prices partly serve this function: new retailers see thin margins and think twice.

punchline.text: Low prices can be a wall, not a gift.

quiz.question: What is the goal of limit pricing?

hook.text: A market with one firm can still be competitive—if potential entrants can enter and exit freely.

buildup.text: In a contestable market, the threat of entry disciplines the monopolist. It prices as if competitors existed.

discovery.text: The key condition: no sunk costs. If entering and exiting costs nothing, hit-and-run entry becomes viable.

twist.text: Airlines were thought to be contestable. But airport gates, brand loyalty, and frequent-flier programs create barriers.

climax.text: Perfectly contestable markets are rare, but the theory shows that potential competition matters as much as actual.

punchline.text: The threat of entry can be enough.

quiz.question: What makes a market 'contestable'?
options: Free entry and exit with no sunk costs

hook.text: Sony and Samsung competed fiercely in TVs—yet jointly invested $2 billion in an LCD factory. Why?

buildup.text: Strategic alliances let rivals share costs, access technology, and enter markets they couldn't crack alone.

discovery.text: Game theory treats alliances as cooperative games: players form coalitions to increase their joint payoff.

twist.text: But alliances are unstable. Each partner is tempted to learn the other's secrets and then compete independently.

climax.text: Successful alliances have clear exit rules, shared information boundaries, and mutual hostage mechanisms.

punchline.text: Cooperate to compete; compete to survive.

quiz.question: Why are strategic alliances between competitors unstable?
options: Partners want to learn secrets and compete independently

hook.text: Why are there only three major credit card networks? Barriers to entry keep new competitors out.

buildup.text: Barriers include patents, brand loyalty, economies of scale, network effects, and regulatory requirements.

discovery.text: In game theory, barriers change the payoff matrix: entry becomes negative-expected-value for newcomers.

twist.text: Some barriers are natural (scale). Others are strategic: incumbents create them deliberately.

climax.text: Tech giants acquire potential rivals early, turning would-be competitors into controlled subsidiaries.

punchline.text: The best monopoly is one nobody can enter.

quiz.question: Which is a strategic barrier to entry?

hook.text: If competitors agree to keep prices high, everyone makes more money. That's the appeal of collusion.

buildup.text: Collusion turns a competitive game into a cooperative one. Firms act as a joint monopoly.

discovery.text: OPEC is the most famous cartel: member nations agree on oil output to maintain high prices.

twist.text: Collusion is a prisoner's dilemma. Each firm profits more by secretly cutting prices while others hold.

climax.text: Cartels almost always collapse. The temptation to cheat is too strong, and cheaters often go undetected.

punchline.text: Cartels are cooperation waiting to fail.

quiz.question: Why do cartels usually collapse?
options: Each member is tempted to secretly cheat

hook.text: What if firms coordinate without ever speaking? Tacit collusion uses signals instead of agreements.

buildup.text: A market leader raises prices. Other firms follow within days. No meeting, no contract, no evidence.

discovery.text: Price leadership works because followers know that matching avoids a destructive price war.

twist.text: Tacit collusion is legal. Antitrust law requires an explicit agreement—parallel behavior alone isn't enough.

climax.text: Airlines, cement, and banking often show parallel pricing. Regulators suspect collusion but can't prove it.

punchline.text: No meeting needed. Just follow the leader.

quiz.question: Why is tacit collusion hard to prosecute?
options: There's no explicit agreement to prove

hook.text: The US DOJ offers a deal: the first cartel member to confess gets full immunity. The rest get fined.

buildup.text: This turns the cartel into a prisoner's dilemma. Each member fears being the last to confess.

discovery.text: Since 1993, leniency programs have uncovered over 100 cartels and generated billions in fines.

twist.text: The program works not because firms are ethical, but because self-interest makes confession optimal.

climax.text: Europe, Japan, and Brazil adopted similar programs. The game theory logic is universal.

punchline.text: Turn cartel members into informants.

quiz.question: How do leniency programs break cartels?
options: By rewarding the first member to confess

hook.text: OPEC controls 40% of global oil. Its members agree on production quotas. Few actually follow them.

buildup.text: Each member benefits from secretly pumping extra barrels. More oil means more revenue—for the cheater.

discovery.text: Saudi Arabia often plays enforcer, cutting its own production to offset others' cheating.

twist.text: In 2020, Saudi Arabia flooded the market to punish Russia for refusing cuts, crashing oil to $20 a barrel.

climax.text: OPEC survives because members need each other, but it limps along—perpetually undermined by defection.

punchline.text: Even among allies, cheating tempts.

quiz.question: Why does Saudi Arabia sometimes flood the oil market?
options: To punish other producers who refuse to cut output

hook.text: Pricing algorithms at competing firms learned to keep prices high without any human coordination.

buildup.text: AI systems trained on market data independently converge on collusive pricing strategies.

discovery.text: Lab experiments confirmed: pricing bots playing repeated games learn tacit collusion on their own.

twist.text: No human agreed to collude. No law was broken. The algorithm discovered it was profitable to cooperate.

climax.text: Regulators worldwide now investigate whether AI pricing should be treated as illegal coordination.

punchline.text: Machines can collude without being told.

quiz.question: What is algorithmic collusion?
options: AI independently learning to keep prices high

hook.text: Pfizer and Moderna raced to develop COVID vaccines. The winner would earn billions. The loser: nothing.

buildup.text: Patent races are all-pay auctions: every firm spends on R&D, but only the winner gets the patent.

discovery.text: The competitive pressure speeds innovation but also causes wasteful duplication of research effort.

twist.text: Firms over-invest when the prize is large. Patent races can burn more resources than the invention is worth.

climax.text: Strategic timing matters: some firms wait until rivals commit, then sprint to finish second-but-better.

punchline.text: Innovation races reward speed over perfection.

quiz.question: Why are patent races compared to all-pay auctions?
options: Every firm spends on R&D but only the winner profits

hook.text: VHS beat Betamax. Blu-ray beat HD DVD. USB-C is beating everything. Standards wars are strategic games.

buildup.text: When a product becomes the standard, network effects lock in customers and lock out competitors.

discovery.text: Firms use strategies like early licensing, bundling, and subsidizing complementary products to win adoption.

twist.text: The better technology doesn't always win. VHS was inferior to Betamax but had better ecosystem strategy.

climax.text: Standards wars are coordination games: everyone benefits from one standard, but which one is the battle.

punchline.text: Standards aren't chosen—they're won.

quiz.question: Why did VHS beat Betamax?

hook.text: Netflix started mailing DVDs. Blockbuster laughed. Then Netflix pivoted to streaming and Blockbuster died.

buildup.text: Disruptors enter with inferior products targeting overlooked segments. Incumbents dismiss them—rationally.

discovery.text: The disruptor improves fast. By the time the incumbent reacts, the game has already shifted.

twist.text: Incumbents can't easily respond: their existing customers, cost structure, and culture resist change.

climax.text: Clayton Christensen's 'Innovator's Dilemma' showed that doing everything right can still mean losing.

punchline.text: The rational response is the fatal one.

quiz.question: Why do incumbents often fail to respond to disruptors?

hook.text: Intel spends $15 billion a year on R&D. This isn't just investment—it's a strategic signal.

buildup.text: Massive R&D spending tells rivals: 'We'll always have the next chip. Don't bother competing.'

discovery.text: The commitment changes the game. Potential competitors divert resources elsewhere, knowing they can't match.

twist.text: But overcommitment to one direction creates blind spots. Nokia's R&D couldn't save it from the iPhone.

climax.text: R&D spending is strategic when it deters entry. It's wasteful when directed at the wrong technology.

punchline.text: Spend to deter, not just to invent.

quiz.question: How does R&D spending serve as strategy beyond innovation?
options: It signals commitment and deters competitors

hook.text: Google gave away Android for free. Why would a firm give away something worth billions?

buildup.text: Open source looks like charity. In game theory, it's a strategic move to commoditize competitors' products.

discovery.text: By giving away the OS, Google ensured its search and ad services reached every smartphone.

twist.text: The strategy only works if you profit from a complement. Android is free; Google Search ads are not.

climax.text: Open source shifts competitive advantage from the shared layer to the proprietary one above or below it.

punchline.text: Give away the razor. Sell the blades.

quiz.question: Why did Google give Android away for free?
options: To ensure Google services reached all smartphones

hook.text: A phone is useless if nobody else has one. More users make each user's experience more valuable.

buildup.text: This is a network effect: the value of a product increases with the number of people using it.

discovery.text: Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb all leveraged network effects to dominate their markets.

twist.text: Network effects create winner-take-all dynamics. Second place often means irrelevance.

climax.text: Once a platform reaches critical mass, the network itself becomes the moat that competitors can't cross.

punchline.text: More users make more users join.

quiz.question: What is a network effect?
options: A product becomes more valuable as more people use it

hook.text: Uber needs both drivers and riders. Without drivers, riders leave. Without riders, drivers leave.

buildup.text: Two-sided platforms must attract both sides simultaneously. It's a coordination game.

discovery.text: The solution: subsidize one side to attract the other. Uber paid drivers generously to build the rider base.

twist.text: Which side to subsidize? Usually the side that's harder to attract or more sensitive to switching.

climax.text: Credit cards solved this decades ago: subsidize cardholders (rewards), charge merchants (fees).

punchline.text: Two sides. One must be subsidized.

quiz.question: What is the chicken-and-egg problem in two-sided markets?
options: Both sides need each other to join first

hook.text: Google has 90% of search. Facebook has 75% of social media. Why do these markets tip to one winner?

buildup.text: Strong network effects create positive feedback: more users attract more users, pushing one firm ahead.

discovery.text: Once a platform leads, switching costs trap users. Your friends are on Facebook, not on the alternative.

twist.text: Winner-take-all isn't inevitable. Uber and Lyft coexist because switching costs for riders are low.

climax.text: The key factor: can users multi-home (use both platforms) or must they commit to one?

punchline.text: When switching hurts, monopolies form.

quiz.question: What enables winner-take-all outcomes?
options: Strong network effects and high switching costs

hook.text: Microsoft killed Netscape by bundling Explorer for free with Windows. Platform envelopment in action.

buildup.text: A dominant platform can enter an adjacent market by bundling the new product with its existing one.

discovery.text: The attacker leverages its installed base. Users get the new product 'for free'—no reason to use the rival.

twist.text: Apple enveloped music players (iPod), maps (Apple Maps), and payments (Apple Pay) into the iPhone.

climax.text: Envelopment is why startups fear competing with tech giants—any successful product can be bundled away.

punchline.text: Bundle it, and the standalone dies.

quiz.question: What is platform envelopment?
options: Bundling a rival's product into your platform for free

hook.text: You use both Uber and Lyft—comparing prices before each ride. That's multihoming.

buildup.text: When users can easily use competing platforms, no platform achieves winner-take-all dominance.

discovery.text: Platforms fight multihoming with loyalty programs, exclusive content, and data lock-in.

twist.text: High switching costs on one side can coexist with low costs on the other—creating asymmetric competition.

climax.text: The EU's Digital Markets Act forces interoperability, lowering switching costs to break platform dominance.

punchline.text: Lock-in is the platform's real product.

quiz.question: What is multihoming?
